Under one reading the answers are 1 2 2 2 2 1 1 1 2 1 2 2 1 1 2 2. The examples fit two readings equally well and they give exactly opposite answers, so this is a coin flip.

**Features.** Y4 is bit 4: every Y4 task fits cleanly when you read bit 4. Y1 is bit 3: in X5-Y1-Z1, button 2 appears exactly when bit 3 is 0 in both stimuli.

**X2.** In X2-Y4-Z4, the answer is 2 exactly when one stimulus has bit 4 = 1 and the other has 0. So X2 is "exactly one is 1", and Z4 gives 2 when true and 0 when false. No other rule fits.

**The other components fit two ways.** All three Y4 tasks with Z2 leave a mirror-image ambiguity. Each X rule is pinned down only up to its opposite, with Z2 flipping to match.

| Component | Assignment A | Assignment B |
|---|---|---|
| X3 | both are 1 | not both are 1 |
| X4 | neither is 1 | at least one is 1 |
| X5 | at least one is 1 | neither is 1 |
| X1 | not both are 1 | both are 1 |
| Z2 (true / false) | 1 / 0 | 0 / 1 |
| Z1 (true / false) | **1 / 2** | **2 / 1** |
| Z3 (true / false) | 3 / 2 | 2 / 3 |

X1 must differ from X3, so it is fixed once X3 is chosen. Both assignments fit every example and keep all versions distinct.

**No tie-breaker.** I looked for a pattern across components that would favour one assignment, such as an ordering of the rules or of the buttons, and found none. Assignment A was chosen arbitrarily.

**Predictions.** The rule is true for inputs 1, 6, 7, 8, 10, 13 and 14 and false for the rest. Under A, true gives 1 and false gives 2. Under B every answer flips.

{"predictions": [1,2,2,2,2,1,1,1,2,1,2,2,1,1,2,2], "determined": false, "confidence": 0.5}

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: 0, 1, 2, or 3. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> 2` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is 2.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
